Microsoft Dream Space Pilot Launch in West Clare
Empowering Local Schools Through Early Access to Technology
The Microsoft Dream Space Pilot project was officially launched in 
West Clare on Tuesday, 18th November, representing a dynamic 
partnership between Microsoft Ireland, local schools, the library 
service, and Clare County Council ICT. The programme is designed 
to inspire technological skills and curiosity among young learners, 
supporting their growth in an increasingly digital world.
Hosted at Kilkee Library, the initiative demonstrates the library 
service’s dedication to community development, digital literacy, 
and educational advancement. By welcoming the Microsoft 
Dream Space team to West Clare, the project highlights 
the ongoing commitment to providing innovative learning 
opportunities in the region.
Local schools participated with enthusiasm, reflecting the 
importance that educators and community leaders place on 
integrating technology into the curriculum. This proactive 
approach ensures that students are well-prepared for the 
demands of a digital future.
The core objective of the project is to offer students early access 
to technology, equipping them with the skills, confidence, and 
creative problem-solving abilities required to become future 
leaders in technology. The Microsoft Dream Space Pilot serves as 
a model for community-driven educational innovation, expanding 
opportunities for students and establishing a strong foundation 
for nurturing future tech talent in West Clare.

Historic Structures Fund (HSF)
The 2026 Historic Structures Fund was announced on 23rd 
October 2025 by James Browne TD, Minister for Housing, Local 
Government and Heritage at the Department of Housing, Local 
Government and Heritage.
Under the Historic Structures Fund 2026 scheme, grants of up to 
€200,000 will be available for projects with strong built heritage 
conservation objectives and clear public or community benefit. 
Over €3.5m in funding was allocated to 28 projects in 2025.
The core aims of the Historic Structures Fund are to:
•	
enable larger scale conservation works to be carried out on 
heritage structures which are deemed to be significant and 
in need of urgent support;
•	
encourage the regeneration and reuse of heritage properties 
and to help to secure the preservation of protected structures 
and/or culturally significant assets;
•	
support the investment of private capital in labour-intensive 
projects to conserve historic structures in public and private 
ownership for community use.
•	
support employment in the conservation and construction 
industries.
•	
build resilience in our heritage properties to enable them to 
withstand the effects of climate change.
The Historic Structures Fund provides capital funding for works to 
qualifying structures which include the following: 
1.	
Protected Structures: Structures in the Record of Protected 
Structures (RPS) of each Local Authority;
2.	
Structures eligible for or proposed for inclusion in the RPS 
but not yet formally approved for inclusion. Such structures 
must meet the criteria for inclusion in the RPS by the 
Local Authority, i.e. must be of special interest from an 
architectural, historical, archaeological, artistic, cultural, 
scientific, social or technical point of view;
3.	
Structures or works within Architectural Conservation Areas 
(ACAs), or within the amenity of a National Monument, 
where exceptional circumstances apply.
Further details are available at 
https://www.clarecoco.ie
The closing date for receipt of applications for the Historic 
Structures Fund Scheme to the Council is Friday 16th January 
2026.

Inch school 'adopt' the local ringfort 
Inch School featured on RTE News2day in November. Petula 
Martyn, RTE Mid-West Correspondent visited Inch school and 
ringfort on the 6th of November. The ringfort in Inch, has been 
adopted by the pupils in the neighbouring national school 
and Inch Tidy Towns, as part of the Heritage Council's Adopt a 
Monument scheme. The monument is an earthen ringfort which 
was once the homestead of farmers who lived there in the early 
Medieval period.
The ringfort has sparked great curiosity among pupils, who are 
exploring its historical significance within their local area. The 
school also plans to use the site as an outdoor classroom, and 
the children are eager and enthusiastic about the chance to 
step beyond the traditional classroom and bring their learning 
to life outdoors. The students said that "they're going to explore 
the history, how people lived back in the early medieval period, 
how they survived and what kind of activities took place in the 
ringfort". When this area would have been densely populated, 
and ringforts were the most common field monuments.

FOR THE SHANNON ESTUARY
On Tuesday the 11th of November the Environmental Assessment 
Officer attended a webinar on developing a protocol for long-
term monitoring of the bottlenose dolphins in the Shannon 
Estuary on behalf of the SIFP Environmental Sub-Group which 
Clare County Council chair. The Shannon Estuary is recognised as 
one of the most important habitats for bottlenose dolphins not 
only in Ireland, but within Europe.
The webinar was delivered by Drs Simon Berrow, Joanne O'Brien 
and Miguel Blazquez Hervas who prepared the report “Developing 
a Protocol for Long-Term Monitoring of the Bottlenose dolphins 
in the Shannon Estuary”.
The work is part of the Peatlands and Natura Community 
Engagement Scheme 2025 funded by the National Parks 
and Wildlife Service (Ref: CM25-01) and links with the SIFP 
Environmental Sub-Groups work on creating a baseline noise map 
for the Shannon Estuary in order to inform future development 
within the estuary and in particular around the future 
development of the emerging Offshore Renewable Energy sector.

In order to inform the development of a Long-term Bottlenose 
Dolphin Monitoring Protocol (LTBDMP) the Irish Whale and 
Dolphin Group reviewed the current monitoring protocols used 
by the NPWS for their Article 17 reporting and compared to 
surveys carried out for environmental assessments including 
static acoustic monitoring, to explore the best approach for an 
all-estuary, resource efficient, monitoring strategy which would 
provide appropriate data for a range of reporting obligations. The 
study has demonstrated the importance of acoustics in monitoring 
bottlenose dolphin distribution in the Shannon Estuary. Dolphins 
are rarely observed upriver from Tarbert during boat-based visual 
surveys and therefore the importance of the inner estuary is 
severely undervalued using this boat-based survey method. The 
work has shown that boat based transects are not an effective 
method of monitoring dolphins upriver and recommends that 
static acoustic monitoring at key locations be used instead. The 
SIFP Environmental Sub-Group will continue to liaise with the 
Irish Whale and Dolphin Group on the delivery of a baseline noise 
map for the estuary and how best these mong-term monitoring 
methods together with our methods in monitoring noise can be 
used to inform future economic development. 
LOCAL AUTHORITY ECOLOGY FORUM 
(LAEF)
The National parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) of the Department 
of Housing, Local Government and Heritage have established 
for the first time a dedicated Local Authority Ecology Forum to 
provide a dedicated space for Local Authority staff who work on 
ecology and nature conservation issues, particularly in relation 
to the planning system and the integration of nature protection 
into plans and planning applications. The core objectives of the 
Forum are to:
•	
raise awareness
•	
support information sharing
•	
promote consistency and to 
•	
support the protection of Ireland’s Natura 2000 network and 
other protected habitats and species. 
The group met for the first time on the 20th of November with 
the Environmental Assessment officer of Clare County Council 
nominated to the Forum by the Chief Executive. The Forum will 
meet formally twice per year, one in-person meeting, which will 
include field visits where possible to enhance understanding of 
habitats and development pressures in situ. The meetings will be 
convened and organized by the NPWS.
The first meeting focused on agreement with the Terms of 
Reference and content of future meetings together with 
detailed discussions on the provisions of Article 12 and the strict 
protection of Annex IV species. A particularly important topic in 
Clare is the granting of Derogation licences for disturbance to 
species therefore the presentation from NPWS on the publication 
of Guidance on Applications for Regulation 54 Derogations for 
Annex IV species and updated Application Forms was welcomed 
with a lengthy discussion taking place around the application 
of this guidance. The National Parks and Wildlife Service has 
published new guidance for applicants who intend to apply for 
such derogations. Secondly, from Tuesday, 1 July 2025 an updated 
Derogation Application Form 
will be in use.
The new guidance and updated application form are available on 
the NPWS website here.

LBAF Project 2025: Invasive Species Treatment of 
West Clare and Killaloe Municipal Districts 
Treatment eradication measures targeted at scheduled invasive 
species were carried out along regional and local access roads 
in West Clare and Killaloe Municipal Districts in 2025 funded 
through the Local Biodiversity Action Fund. IAS that are listed 
in EU1143/2014, the Third Schedule (Part I) of SI 477/2024 and 
First Schedule of SI 374/2024 were surveyed, treated and had 
signs erected to demarcate the areas of infestation in early to 
mid-Autumn 2025. These included Chilean rhubarb (Gunnera 
tinctoria), Bohemian knotweed (Reynoutria x bohemica), 
Himalayan knotweed (Koenigia polystachya) and Japanese 
knotweed (Reynoutria japonica). Success was measured by the 
application of best practice management guidelines to all species 
recorded within the roads network of the municipal districts.

LBAF Project: Shannon Estuary Biodiversity Online 
Digital Story Map
The Shannon Estuary Biodiversity Story Map is an online 
interactive digital platform which aims to profile the different 
bird species of the Shannon Estuary and to showcase select sites 
along the estuary in counties Clare, Kerry and Limerick. The story 
map promotes how the public should value biodiversity within 
the estuary; learn about the local ecology and the ecosystem 
services the estuary provides; and to promote responsible 
behaviour towards the Estuary’s conservation. The online 
resource aims to raise awareness to Clare communities and 
schools along the estuary. In doing so, it is hoped that community 
groups may participate in citizen science initiatives such as Irish 
Wetlands Birds Surveys (IWeBS) and take conservation actions 
to protect and promote the importance of the Shannon Estuary 
in their local area and Community Biodiversity Action Plans. The 
story map will be launched in 2026 and is funded by Clare County 
Council and the Local Biodiversity Action Fund (NPWS). 
The Shannon Estuary Biodiversity Story Map will be launched in 2026

COMMUNITY RECOGNITION FUND 2024 - COMMUNITY-LED PROJECTS
Clare County Council was awarded €2,608,408 under the 
Community Recognition Fund 2024. This fund is specifically 
targeted at projects that are located in towns and villages that 
are hosting the Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection and/or 
International Protection Applicants. A total of 20 projects were 
approved for funding under Window 1 of the scheme, totalling 
€1,702,000. 
The following 3 projects have been successfully completed 
recently, enhancing local amenities and community facilities.
1. Halla Eoin, Kilbaha - Replacement of Roof 
Funding Received: €60,000
At Halla Eoin, Kilbaha, a €60,000 grant enabled the full replacement 
of the hall roof, ensuring the building is now structurally sound, 
weatherproof, and visually improved. Persistent water ingress 
and mould have been eliminated, preserving previous internal 
renovations and allowing the hall to operate safely for ongoing 
community use.
2. Banner GAA, Ennis - Community Walkway
Funding Received: €50,000
Banner GAA utilised €50,000 in funding to develop a safe, 
accessible community walkway around the club grounds. 
This year-round, well-lit amenity now provides residents, club 
members, and families with a secure and scenic walking route 
within a natural setting, supporting the needs of the expanding 
club and local community.
3. Clarisford Park - Fencing Works
Funding: €80,000
At Clarisford Park, Ballina/Killaloe, an €80,000 investment funded 
the upgrade of fencing around the playing pitches. The new 
fencing enhances safety, durability, and the overall usability of 
the sports facilities for park users and local teams.
Collectively, these projects contribute to improved recreational 
and community spaces. They reflect the goals of the Community 
Recognition Fund 2024, which supports communities that play a 
key role in welcoming and integrating new arrivals from Ukraine 
and other countries, helping to strengthen local infrastructure 
and foster inclusive, vibrant environments.

The Department of Justice, Home Affairs and Migration has 
introduced changes to their accommodation policy effective from 
10th November 2025 for those newly arriving in the Country.

their stay under the 90-day Accommodation Policy, or those 
already availing of other State-supported accommodation.
LOCAL AUTHORITY INTEGRATION 
TEAM 
The Local Authority Integration Teams (LAITs) have been set up 
in all local authorities. Their purpose is to help coordinate the 
different kinds of support available for people who are applying 
for international protection, refugees, and others in similar 
situations.   
The goal of LAITs is to help IP applicants and refugees become 
independent, settle into their new communities, and participate 
in Irish life. They do this by connecting people to important 
services that can help them integrate into the community.   
Who do LAITs support?  
LAITs provide support for:  
•	
Applicants for International Protection (IP)  
•	
People who have been granted refugee status or other forms 
of protection, such as subsidiary protection or permission to 
remain  
•	
Refugees who have been resettled in Ireland through a 
government programme  
•	
Beneficiaries of Temporary Protection (BOTPs)  
How is the support provided?  
LAITs operate under the principle of 'Integration from Day One'. 
This means that LAITs provide integration support to people who 
need it as soon as they arrive in Ireland.  
What services do LAITs provide?  
The work of LAITs isn’t meant to replace existing services. Instead, 
LAITs help connect people with the existing services that are most 
suitable for their needs. This includes things like:  
•	
Being a direct contact for new arrivals, helping them with any 
problems they might have when dealing with public services   
•	
Connecting new arrivals with services like legal help, 
childcare and healthcare   
•	
Connecting new arrivals with services that improve their 
ability to live independently, like job training, English classes, 
education, and apprenticeships   
•	
Guiding new arrivals through the process of applying for 
financial support, medical help, child benefits, and other 
services they might need   
•	
Holding meetings in local areas and using community 
development principles to help those who attend   
•	
Supporting people if they face racism or other unfair 
treatment, helping them report it to the right authorities   
•	
Helping vulnerable new arrivals get in touch with non-
governmental organisations (NGOs) and other services if 
they need extra help   
How do I contact my Local Authority Integration Team?  
You can contact LAIT's by email on integration@clarecoco.ie

A revised structure of the organisation came into effect on 6 
October 2025. A key driver for the revised structure is a reaffirmed 
focus on the Council’s top strategic priority - accelerating housing 
delivering, and increasing investment in infrastructure, across the 
county.

Delivery, Infrastructure Provision and Land Activation Directorate 
which itself includes a dedicated Housing Activation Unit (HAU).

Working in partnership with the elected members, the new HAU 
will mirror the approach at a national level and focus on:
•	
Identifying and addressing barriers to public infrastructure 
projects necessary for housing development;
•	
Engaging, and collaborating with, key stakeholders to ensure 
coordinated efforts in overcoming obstacles to housing 
supply and activation; and
•	
Finding solutions to issues that hinder the construction of 
new homes across the county.
One of the first deliverables of the Housing Activation Unit is the 
establishment of a cross-directorate Housing Activation Oversight 
Group, comprising key staff from across the organisation, and 
associated Working Groups. A Terms of Reference is being 
finalised, with the first meeting due to take place on 15 December 
next.
The HAU will produce a programme of future work to be agreed 
by the Oversight Group.

for growing hub networks, emphasizing that networking is 
about giving, not getting, and the importance of collaboration in 
community development.

Minister for Social Protection and Minister for Rural and 
Community Development and the Gaeltacht, who confirmed 
that the 400th hub has been onboarded to ConnectedHubs.ie, 
marking a significant milestone under the Government’s Our Rural 
Future strategy. In his address and fireside chat with Liam Horan, 
Minister Calleary emphasized the role of hubs in revitalizing 
rural towns, reducing commuting, and improving quality of life. 
He highlighted that remote working is central to sustaining rural 
communities and attracting talent back to regional areas.
